unit_label: ABFM Module D unit 1 (courseware unit 19): hybrid finance

facts.statement: Hybrid securities (courseware): a security combining characteristics of debt and equity in one instrument is a hybrid. Hybrids allow more flexibility to postpone payment than traditional debt and can benefit investors, shareholders and issuers; they let companies tune the proportion of debt to equity in the capital structure. Types: preference shares, warrants, convertible debentures or bonds, foreign currency convertible bonds and mezzanine financing. Advantages: higher yield than debt for investors, lower price volatility than equity because there is a regular pre-determined return, and risk diversification for the issuer because they have no strict definition of equity or debt. Disadvantage: assessment is difficult because the return is not as simple to calculate as on equity or bonds. A hybrid is called innovative if its reward is linked to a general economic variable such as an interest rate, exchange rate or commodities index.

Preference share capital (courseware): preference shareholders have a priority claim over equity shareholders on income and on assets. The dividend is at a fixed rate and must be paid before any dividend to equity holders, but preference holders have no legal right to compel payment and cannot push the company into bankruptcy for missing it. On liquidation they are repaid before equity holders. Classes may rank as senior or junior to other classes. Preference shares may be issued with or without a maturity date; perpetual (irredeemable) shares have none. Credit rating agencies can rate preference share issues. The Companies Act definition: preference share capital carries a preferential right to payment of a dividend at a fixed amount or rate and to repayment of capital on winding up, with or without a premium, and capital that also has rights to participate in dividends or surplus beyond the preferential rights is still preference capital if it carries those preferential rights.

Kinds of preference share (courseware): cumulative (unpaid dividends accumulate and must be cleared before any equity dividend; shown as a contingent liability); non-cumulative (a missed dividend is forfeited, with no arrears); participating (a fixed dividend plus a share in surplus profits after equity holders have received a stated rate, and a share of surplus on winding up); non-participating (only the fixed dividend and the preference amount on winding up); redeemable (repaid after a set period or at the issuer option, possibly with a call option); non-redeemable (repaid only on liquidation); convertible (convertible into equity at the holder option on stated terms); non-convertible (no conversion right unless stated); adjustable-rate (dividend is linked to prevailing market interest rates rather than fixed).

Purpose and redemption of preference shares (courseware): reasons to issue them are improved access to capital in an uninteresting primary market, avoiding the need for security (no charge such as a mortgage), freedom from deposit regulations, flexible and medium-term maturity, and dividends that can be skipped in a loss year, unlike interest on debentures. Preference capital became more attractive when the dividend was tax-exempt in the hands of investors; the willingness of investors to accept a lower dividend lowered its cost, and it suits firms with good records that are near their debt limits. Redemption is repaying the capital at a date fixed at issue (the maturity date) or earlier by call. To protect the interest of outsiders, redemption of fully paid preference shares must not reduce shareholders funds: the company either redeems out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares, or transfers distributable profits to a capital redemption reserve of equal amount, which can only be used to issue bonus shares so that shareholder funds return to the same level. A company issuing fresh shares at a premium may use the securities premium account only for specified purposes, such as fully paid bonus shares, preliminary expenses, issue costs and premium on redemption.

Perpetual non-cumulative preference shares of banks (courseware, principles only): banks issue them as part of Additional Tier 1 capital. Features: issued by the bank and fully paid, with no maturity date, step-up or other redemption incentive; dividends fixed or floating by reference to a market rate, fully discretionary and not cumulative; no put option for the investor; a call option only after a minimum period and with the regulator consent, exercisable only if the bank replaces the capital or has well above minimum capital; repayment only with regulator approval; claims rank senior to equity but subordinated to depositors and general creditors; may absorb losses through conversion to common shares or a write-down at a trigger point. The bank must not buy or lend against them. The percentages, limits and conditions given in the courseware are not taught.

Warrants (courseware): the holder has the right but not the obligation to buy a set number of equity shares at a fixed price during a set period. Warrants are sometimes attached to debt instruments to sweeten the terms, and are issued to promoters and institutional investors on a preferential basis to let them raise their stake if the firm performs well. A warrant carries no dividend or voting rights until it is converted into shares; only then does the investor get those rights. Where warrants are issued on a preferential basis the buyer pays part of the price up front, which is adjusted against the final payment and is forfeited if the warrant is not exercised. To protect minority shareholders, the pre-fixed conversion price in a preferential issue cannot be below a floor based on recent market prices (the specific averaging periods are not taught).

Convertible debentures (courseware): a debenture that can be converted into equity shares in whole or in part is a convertible debenture (fully convertible FCD or partly convertible PCD). The conversion terms must be disclosed, including the conversion premium and timing. The conversion ratio is the number of equity shares received for each debenture and the conversion price is the par value divided by the conversion ratio; for example a Rs 100 debenture convertible into five shares has a conversion ratio of 5 and a conversion price of Rs 20. At issue the conversion price is usually set 20 to 30 per cent above the market price, and the ratio and price stay unchanged during the life, but there is usually a clause protecting holders from dilution caused by bonus issues, share splits and the sale of equity at prices below the conversion price. In India, convertible debentures have been regulated since the early 1990s, and the courseware notes three forms: automatically converting after a period, optional conversion within a period, and conversion after a longer period with put and call features. The courseware states time limits and rating requirements which are not taught.

Warrants versus convertible debentures (courseware): both give a call option on equity. The option in a convertible debenture cannot be separated from the debenture, whereas a warrant attached to a debenture can be detached; warrants can be issued on their own; warrants normally need a cash payment to exercise, whereas conversion of a convertible is just an accounting transfer, so exercising warrants brings new capital into the company while conversion does not; most convertibles carry a call provision that lets the issuer refund the debt or force conversion depending on whether the conversion value is above or below the call price, while warrants usually cannot be cancelled; convertibles often have more time before they expire than warrants. For warrants on a preferential issue, an upfront amount is forfeited if not exercised; no forfeiture applies in the case of optionally convertible debentures.

Valuation of warrants (courseware): a warrant is like a call option on the equity of the issuer, so option methods apply. The maximum value is the stock price less the exercise price; the warrant price lies between the lower limit and the upper limit. Its premium over the minimum value depends on the volatility of the stock price, the time remaining before expiry, the risk-free interest rate, the stock price and the exercise price. The Black-Scholes model gives the value as C = S x N(d1) - E x e^(-rt) x N(d2), with d1 = [ln(S/E) + (r + sigma^2/2) t] / (sigma x sqrt(t)) and d2 = d1 - sigma x sqrt(t), where S is the stock price, E the exercise price, r the continuously compounded risk-free rate, t the time to expiry in years, sigma the annual standard deviation of the stock return and N the cumulative standard normal distribution. The method assumes no dividends and ignores dilution caused by the exercise of the warrants. The steps: calculate d1 and d2; find N(d1) and N(d2); find the present value of the exercise price, E divided by e^(rt); and substitute.

Valuation of convertible debentures (courseware): a partly convertible debenture has three parts: interest throughout the life, equity shares received on part conversion and the repayment of the non-convertible part of principal. Its value is the present value of the interest at the investor required return on debt, plus the present value of the expected value of equity shares received at the investor required return on equity, plus the present value of principal instalments at the required return on debt. The cost to the issuer uses the after-tax interest and discounts at the cost of capital, solving for the rate that equates the net subscription price with the discounted flows. An optionally convertible debenture is valued like a compulsorily convertible one, but the market may pay a premium for the option to decline conversion; its value can never be less than that of a similar compulsorily convertible debenture.

Why issue warrants and convertibles (courseware): conventional explanations are that they make inexpensive debt possible and that they let firms sell equity later at a price above today price; the courseware says these explanations do not hold up. Modern finance explanations: matching of cash flows (low initial interest burden suits a developing, risky firm; if it succeeds, holders convert and dilution is welcome), financial synergy (when the risk of the issuer cannot be assessed, a convertible is a package of a straight debenture and a call option whose values move opposite ways: a risky firm has a low debenture value and a high option value, a safe firm the reverse, so required returns do not depend heavily on the risk estimate), and reduction of agency costs (equity holders favour risky projects, bondholders safe ones; holders of convertibles share in the upside, so they care less about risk-taking and covenants can be lighter).

Foreign currency convertible bond (courseware): a FCCB is a bond issued in a foreign currency (the US dollar is the most common), combining debt and equity: regular coupon and principal, with an option to convert into equity at a set conversion price. Holders convert only if the share price is above the conversion price; otherwise they redeem at maturity. It often includes a call option for the issuer and a put option for the holder. Because of the conversion option the coupon is lower than on a plain bond, so it is cheaper than equity and cheaper than straight debt on a coupon basis, but the issuer carries exchange rate risk (a weaker rupee raises the cost of servicing coupons and principal), political, economic and legal risks of the country, and, if the holders do not convert, must repay the principal at maturity. Typical term is about five years. Holders bear exchange rate and credit risk; if the issuer fails, the principal is not repaid.

Mezzanine financing (courseware): a hybrid of debt and equity that gives the lender the right to convert the debt into equity in case of default. It is used for specific projects or acquisitions, offers higher returns to investors, is often unsecured, may have partly fixed and partly variable interest, and typically matures in more than five years, depending on the maturity of existing debt. For the issuer it is more expensive than debt or equity from some perspectives, since it ranks below senior debt, but cheaper than equity because its cost is below the cost of equity; it is carried in the books as debt of the issuing company.

Innovative hybrids (courseware): these combine a conventional debt or equity security with a derivative such as a forward, swap or option. Categories illustrated: convertible bearer eurobonds (a lower coupon than comparable straight bonds), commodity-linked bonds (the repayment is tied to a commodity price such as oil, giving the holder a payoff linked to the price above a base level), dual-currency bonds (interest in one currency and principal fixed in another, to manage exchange risk), collared floating rate notes (a floating rate with a floor and a cap, the investor accepting a cap in return for an above-market rate), and rating-sensitive notes (the spread rises if the issuer debt rating falls, reducing disputes between bondholders and shareholders). The courseware attributes the growth of hybrids to completing markets and to tax or regulatory benefits, and notes the criticism that many are supply-driven fads pushed by investment bankers.

payload.title: Hybrid securities: meaning, types, advantages and drawbacks
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **hybrid security** combines **debt and equity features** in one instrument, giving **flexibility to postpone payment** and letting the issuer tune its **debt-equity mix**.

**Types:** **preference shares**, **warrants**, **convertible debentures or bonds**, **foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCB)**, **mezzanine financing**.

| Advantages | Disadvantage |
| --- | --- |
| **Higher yield than debt** | **Hard to assess**: return is **not as simple to calculate** as on equity or bonds |
| **Less price volatility than equity** (regular, pre-determined return) |  |
| **Risk diversification** for the issuer (**no strict definition** as debt or equity) |  |

A hybrid is **innovative** when its reward is **linked to an economic variable** such as an **interest rate, exchange rate or commodity index**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Hybrids sit between the two extremes of debt and equity on the financing spectrum.

self_check.prompt_text: What makes a hybrid security innovative?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Its return is tied to a broad economic variable, for example an interest rate, an exchange rate or a commodity index.

payload.title: Preference share capital
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Preference shareholders** have a **priority claim** over equity holders on **income** (a **fixed-rate dividend** paid **before** equity) and on **assets** in **liquidation**.

**But:** they have **no legal right to force payment** and **cannot push the company into bankruptcy** for a missed dividend.

**Companies Act idea:** capital with a **preferential right to a fixed dividend** and to **repayment of capital on winding up** is **preference capital**; extra participation rights do not change that.

Preference shares may be **issued with or without maturity**; **perpetual (irredeemable)** shares have none. **Classes** can be **senior or junior** to each other. **Rating agencies** can rate them.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Preference capital ranks after all creditors but before equity.

self_check.prompt_text: Can preference shareholders force a company into bankruptcy for a missed dividend?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, they have no legal right to compel payment of the dividend.

payload.title: Kinds of preference shares
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Kind | Feature |
| --- | --- |
| **Cumulative** | **Unpaid dividends accumulate** (arrears) and must be paid **before any equity dividend** |
| **Non-cumulative** | A **missed dividend is lost**; no arrears |
| **Participating** | **Fixed dividend plus a share in surplus profits** after equity holders get a stated rate (and surplus on winding up) |
| **Non-participating** | **Only the fixed dividend** and the **preference amount** on winding up |
| **Redeemable** | **Repaid** after a set period or earlier at the **issuer option** |
| **Non-redeemable** | Repaid only on **liquidation** |
| **Convertible** | Can be **converted to equity** at the holder option |
| **Non-convertible** | **No conversion right** unless stated |
| **Adjustable-rate** | Dividend **linked to market interest rates**, not fixed |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Cumulative shares are more valuable to holders than non-cumulative ones because arrears are not lost.

self_check.prompt_text: What happens to a missed dividend on non-cumulative preference shares?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is forfeited for that year, with no arrears carried forward.

payload.title: Why issue preference shares, and how they are redeemed
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Reasons to issue:** **no security** (no charge on assets) needed, **deposit regulations do not apply**, **flexible medium-term maturity**, and **dividends can be skipped** in a loss year (unlike **interest**). They suit **good-record firms near their debt limit**.

**Cost:** **dividend / issue price**; dividends are **not tax-deductible**, so there is **no interest tax shield**.

**Redemption** must **not reduce shareholder funds**: either **redeem out of a fresh issue of shares** or **transfer distributable profits to a Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR)**, usable **only for bonus shares**. **CRR transfer = nominal value redeemed - proceeds of fresh issue applied**.

**Securities premium** from a fresh issue may be used only for **specified purposes** (for example **bonus shares**, **preliminary expenses**, **issue costs**, **premium on redemption**).

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{CRR transfer} = \text{Nominal value redeemed} - \text{Fresh issue proceeds applied}

variables.name: Nominal value of the preference shares redeemed
Proceeds of a fresh issue used for the redemption

common_errors: Treating the transfer as a distribution to shareholders

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The reserve keeps outsiders protected by leaving the same level of capital behind after redemption.

self_check.prompt_text: What may the Capital Redemption Reserve be used for?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Only to issue fully paid bonus shares.

payload.title: Perpetual non-cumulative preference shares of banks
payload.core_explanation_md:
Banks issue **perpetual non-cumulative preference shares (PNCPS)** as part of **Additional Tier 1 capital**.

**Principles:** **issued by the bank**, **fully paid**; **no maturity**, **no step-up**, **no incentive to redeem**; **dividends fully discretionary** and **not cumulative**; **no put option**; a **call only after a minimum period**, **with regulator consent**, and only if the capital is **replaced** or well above the minimum; **repayment needs regulator approval**; **ranks above equity** but **below depositors and creditors**; **loss-absorbing** through **conversion to common shares or write-down at a trigger**.

The **limits and percentages** in the courseware are **not taught** because they are revised.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: These features make the instrument behave like permanent capital that can absorb a bank loss.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a bank cancel dividends on PNCPS without default?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The dividends are fully discretionary and non-cumulative, so cancellation is not a default.

payload.title: Features of warrants
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **warrant** gives the holder the **right, not the obligation**, to buy a **fixed number of equity shares** at a **fixed price** within a **set period**.

- Often **attached to debt** to **sweeten** the terms, or issued to **promoters and institutions** on a **preferential basis** to raise their stake if the firm does well.
- **No dividend or voting rights** until **converted into shares**.
- **Preferential issue:** part of the price is **paid up front**, **adjusted** against the final payment and **forfeited** if the warrant is **not exercised**.
- To protect **minority holders**, the **conversion price** in a preferential issue **cannot be below a floor** linked to **recent market prices** (periods not taught).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because the holder can walk away, the upfront amount is the issuer protection against a non-exercise.

self_check.prompt_text: Do warrant holders receive dividends before exercise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, they have no dividend or voting rights until the warrant is converted into shares.

payload.title: Convertible debentures: conversion ratio and conversion price
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **convertible debenture** can be turned into **equity shares**, in **full (FCD)** or **part (PCD)**. Conversion **terms** (ratio, price, timing, premium) are **disclosed**.

**Conversion ratio (CR) = number of shares per debenture.**
**Conversion price = par value / CR.**
**Conversion value = CR x current share price.**
**Conversion premium = (conversion price - market price) / market price.**

Example pattern: a **Rs 100 debenture** convertible into **5 shares** has **CR 5** and **conversion price Rs 20**.

At issue the conversion price is usually **20 to 30 per cent above the market price**; ratio and price **stay fixed**, with a clause **protecting holders against dilution** from **bonus issues, splits and low-priced equity sales**.

assumptions: The ratio is fixed at issue
Anti-dilution adjustments are applied if needed
common_errors: Dividing the market price by the ratio
Confusing conversion price with the market price

payload.expanded_explanation_md: The conversion premium measures how far the share price must rise before conversion pays.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the conversion price computed?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The par value of the debenture divided by the conversion ratio.

payload.title: Warrants versus convertible debentures
payload.core_explanation_md:
Both give a **call option on equity**. Differences:

| Point | Warrant | Convertible debenture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Separability** | Can be **detached** from an attached debenture | Option **cannot be separated** |
| **Standalone issue** | **Yes** | No: it is a debt instrument |
| **Exercise** | **Cash payment**: **new capital** enters the firm | **Accounting transfer** only: **no new capital** |
| **Call provision** | Usually **cannot be cancelled** | Most carry an **issuer call** to **refund or force conversion** |
| **Life** | Usually **shorter** | Often **longer** |
| **Forfeiture** | Upfront payment **forfeited** if not exercised (preferential issue) | **None** for optionally convertible debentures |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Exercise of a warrant raises money; conversion of a debenture only swaps debt for equity.

self_check.prompt_text: Which instrument brings new capital into the company when the option is used?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A warrant, because the holder pays the exercise price in cash.

payload.title: Valuation of a warrant: bounds and the Black-Scholes model
payload.core_explanation_md:
A warrant is a **call option** on the issuer equity.

**Intrinsic value = max(S - E, 0)**. The **maximum** value of a warrant is the **stock price**; the **lower bound** is the **intrinsic value**. The price lies between.

**Premium over the minimum rises with:** **volatility**, **time to expiry**, **risk-free rate** and **stock price**; **it falls with the exercise price**.

**Black-Scholes:** **C = S x N(d1) - E x e^(-rt) x N(d2)**

**d1 = [ln(S/E) + (r + sigma^2 / 2) t] / (sigma x sqrt t)**; **d2 = d1 - sigma x sqrt t**.

**Steps:** 1) find **d1 and d2**; 2) read **N(d1) and N(d2)** from tables; 3) compute **E / e^(rt)**; 4) **substitute**.

**Limits:** assumes **no dividends** and **ignores dilution** from exercise.

formula_spec.latex_expression: C = S N(d_1) - E e^{-rt} N(d_2)
assumptions: No dividends are paid before expiry
common_errors: Using the simple rate instead of the continuous rate
Using E instead of its present value in the second term

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A larger volatility or longer life raises the value because the option has limited downside.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two limits of applying Black-Scholes to a warrant.
self_check.expected_takeaway: It ignores dividends and the dilution caused when warrants are exercised.

payload.title: Valuing and costing convertible debentures
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **partly convertible debenture** has **three parts**: **interest** through the life, **equity shares** on part conversion and **repayment of the non-convertible principal**.

**Value to the investor** = **PV of interest at the required return on debt** + **PV of the expected value of the shares received at the required return on equity** + **PV of principal instalments at the required return on debt**.

**Cost to the issuer:** use **after-tax interest** and find the rate that **equates the net subscription price to the discounted flows**.

**Optionally convertible:** valued like a **compulsorily convertible** one, but the market may pay a **premium for the option to decline conversion**; its value **can never be below** that of a similar compulsorily convertible debenture.

variables.name: Expected value of shares received at conversion

assumptions: Cash flows are certain in timing
common_errors: Discounting the share value at the debt rate
Ignoring the tax shield in the issuer cost

payload.expanded_explanation_md: Each part is discounted at the rate that fits its risk: debt flows at the debt rate and shares at the equity rate.

self_check.prompt_text: At what rate is the expected value of shares received on conversion discounted?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At the investor required return on equity.

payload.title: Why companies issue warrants and convertibles
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Conventional explanations:** **cheap debt** and **selling equity later at a higher price**. The courseware says these are **not persuasive**.

**Modern finance explanations:**

- **Matching of cash flows:** the **low initial interest burden** suits a **developing, risky** firm; if it succeeds, holders **convert** and **dilution is welcome**.
- **Financial synergy:** when the issuer **risk is hard to assess**, a convertible is a **straight debenture plus a call option** whose values **move in opposite directions**: a **risky** firm has a **low debenture value and a high option value**, a **safe** firm the reverse, so the **required return is not very sensitive** to the risk estimate.
- **Agency costs:** **equity holders favour risk, bondholders safety**; convertible holders **share the upside**, so they worry less about **risk-taking** and **covenants can be lighter**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The two parts of a convertible hedge each other, which makes it easier to price an uncertain issuer.

self_check.prompt_text: How does a convertible reduce the conflict between bondholders and shareholders?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Convertible holders share the upside of risk-taking, so they care less about the company taking risk.

payload.title: Foreign currency convertible bonds
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **FCCB** is a bond in a **foreign currency** (often the **US dollar**) with **coupon and principal** plus an **option to convert into equity** at a **set conversion price**.

- Holders **convert only if the share price is above the conversion price**; otherwise they **redeem** at maturity.
- Often has an **issuer call** and a **holder put**.
- **Coupon is lower** than on a straight bond because of the option, so the **cost to the issuer is lower**.
- **Risks to the issuer:** **exchange rate** (a weaker rupee raises the servicing cost), **country, political and legal risks**, and **repayment at maturity** if holders do not convert.
- Typical **term about five years**.
- Holders carry **exchange rate and credit risk**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The cheap coupon can be wiped out if the rupee falls against the bond currency.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the FCCB coupon lower than on a plain bond?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Investors accept less because the conversion option has value.

payload.title: Mezzanine financing
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Mezzanine finance** is a **hybrid of debt and equity**: the **lender can convert the debt into equity if the borrower defaults**.

- Used for **specific projects or acquisitions**.
- **Higher returns** for the investor; often **unsecured**.
- Interest may be **partly fixed and partly variable**.
- Usually matures in **more than five years**, in line with the **existing debt**.
- In the issuer books it is carried as **debt**.
- It ranks **below senior debt**, so it is **costlier than senior debt** but **cheaper than equity**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: It fills the gap between senior loans and pure equity in the financing stack.

self_check.prompt_text: What right does a mezzanine lender have on default?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The right to convert the debt into equity.

payload.title: Innovative hybrids
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Innovative hybrids** combine a **bond or share** with a **derivative** (forward, swap or option).

| Hybrid | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Convertible bearer eurobond** | **Lower coupon** than comparable straight bonds |
| **Commodity-linked bond** | **Repayment tied to a commodity price** above a base level |
| **Dual-currency bond** | **Interest in one currency, principal in another**, to manage **exchange risk** |
| **Collared floating-rate note** | **Floating rate with a floor and cap**; the investor accepts the cap for a **higher rate** |
| **Rating-sensitive note** | **Spread rises if the issuer rating falls**, easing **bondholder-shareholder disputes** |

**Why they spread:** they **complete markets** and may offer **tax or regulatory benefits**. **Critics** call many a **supply-driven fad** pushed by bankers.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A collar limits both the downside and the upside for the investor.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a collar on a floating-rate note do?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It sets a minimum rate (floor) and a maximum rate (cap) on the coupon.

payload.stem_md: A convertible debenture of face value Rs 600 can be converted at Rs 40 per share. What is the conversion ratio (shares per debenture)?
A Rs 100 debenture converts into 8 equity shares. What is the conversion price (Rs, to 1 decimal place)?
The conversion price of a debenture is Rs 30 and the share now trades at Rs 24. What is the conversion premium (per cent)?
A debenture converts into 15 shares and the share price is Rs 52. What is the conversion value (Rs)?
A warrant allows its holder to buy a share at Rs 65. The share price is Rs 90. What is the minimum (intrinsic) value of the warrant (Rs)?
A warrant allows its holder to buy a share at Rs 55 but the share price is Rs 40. What is the intrinsic value of the warrant (Rs)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The share price is below the exercise price, so intrinsic value is max(40 - 55, 0) = 0.

payload.stem_md: A warrant has S = Rs 80, E = Rs 75, t = 1 year, r = 6 per cent and sigma = 30 per cent. What is the present value of the exercise price, E e^(-rt) (Rs, to 2 decimal places)?
For the same warrant (S = Rs 80, E = Rs 75, t = 1, r = 6 per cent, sigma = 30 per cent) what is d1 (to 2 decimal places)?
Using Black-Scholes with the same inputs (N(d1) = 0.7140 and N(d2) = 0.6045), what is the value of the warrant (Rs, to 2 decimal places)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: C = 80 x 0.7140 - 70.63 x 0.6045 = 57.12 - 42.70 = about Rs 14.42 (using unrounded N values).

payload.stem_md: A company has Rs 50 crore of 8 per cent cumulative preference shares. Dividends were not paid for 3 years. What are the arrears (Rs crore)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Annual dividend = 0.08 x 50 = Rs 4 crore. Arrears for 3 years = Rs 12 crore.

payload.stem_md: A company issues preference shares at Rs 90 each paying a dividend of Rs 9 a year. What is the cost of this preference capital (per cent)?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Cost = dividend / price = 9 / 90 = 10 per cent, with no tax shield.

payload.stem_md: A company redeems preference shares of nominal value Rs 50 crore and applies the proceeds of a fresh issue of Rs 20 crore. How much distributable profit must be transferred to the capital redemption reserve (Rs crore)?
A company issued 2 lakh warrants, each entitling the holder to buy one share at Rs 120. If all are exercised, how much new capital is raised (Rs lakh)?

A debenture pays interest of Rs 10 a year for 3 years and is then fully converted into shares expected to be worth Rs 130. The investor requires 10 per cent on debt and 15 per cent on equity. What is its value (Rs, to 2 decimal places)?

A company issues a 5-year FCCB of USD 10 million when the exchange rate is Rs 82 per dollar. At maturity the rate is Rs 83.5 and the bond is redeemed. By how much (Rs crore) does the rupee cost of repaying the principal exceed what it would have been at issue?
payload.correct_explanation_md: Extra cost = 10 million x (83.5 - 82) = Rs 15 million = Rs 1.5 crore.

payload.stem_md: A collared floating rate note has a floor of 7 per cent and a cap of 11 per cent. The reference rate for the period is 12 per cent. What coupon rate (per cent) is paid?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The floating rate of 12 per cent exceeds the cap, so the coupon is capped at 11 per cent.

unresolved: The courseware gives many regulatory particulars for hybrid instruments in India: Companies Act 2013 provisions on preference shares (section numbers, the maximum tenor, voting rights after unpaid dividends, application of the securities premium account), the terms of perpetual non-cumulative preference shares as bank Additional Tier 1 capital (percentages of risk-weighted assets, call option conditions, investor limits), the SEBI preferential allotment rules for warrants (upfront payment, pricing floors) and SEBI conditions for convertible debentures (conversion periods, rating requirements). No primary source was retrieved, these rules have been revised more than once and the courseware text appears to mix older and newer regimes, so none of these figures is taught or tested. Only the instrument features and the principles are taught.

The courseware table of external commercial borrowing, foreign currency convertible bond and rupee denominated bond approvals (January 2021 to September 2022) and the named issues (Man Finance, Tata Iron and Steel 1989, TISCO, Carlton, Standard Oil, Sperry, Salomon Brothers, Hanover) are narrative illustrations; they were not checked and are not taught or tested as facts.

The courseware Black-Scholes example (Rs 125 stock, Rs 100 exercise, 0.50 year, 40 per cent volatility, 8 per cent rate, value Rs 31.86) was recomputed and agrees to the second decimal; new inputs are used. The courseware itself states the model ignores dilution and dividends; that limit is taught.

The courseware value formula for a partly convertible debenture and its cost-of-issue version are taught in words and as simple present value arrangements; the symbols for equity shares per debenture and expected price are rearranged.

The courseware statement that convertible debentures and warrants give "the air of offering something for nothing" is taught as the courseware view that the conventional explanations are not persuasive.

The courseware states that perpetual preference shares are "never issued with a maturity" and also that irredeemable preference shares are not permitted for Indian companies; both are courseware statements and the second is not taught as a rule.
Numbers in the numerical items are invented and are checked in tests/content/batch-abfm-d-u01-b001.test.ts, including a recomputation of the Black-Scholes value.
